parts.title: Part 1
parts.context: A student phones a landlady to ask about renting a room in a shared house.
script: Oh, hello. My name's Callum. I'm calling about the room in a shared house that you advertised on the university noticeboard.
Ah yes, the room at Marchmont Road. Let me just find my notes. Right, I'll take a few details first, if that's all right. What's your surname, Callum?
Thank you. And you're a student at the university, I assume?
That's right, I'm in my second year. I'm doing geology. I actually started out in chemistry, but I switched after the first term.

Geology, lovely. We've had a few geologists in the house over the years. They're always away on field trips, so it's quite peaceful. Now, the address is 27 Marchmont Road. That's M-A-R-C-H-M-O-N-T. Do you know it?
I think so. Is that the one near the park?
That's the one, just across from the park gates.
Great. Which floor is the room on? The advert didn't say.
Well, the room on the first floor was taken last week, I'm afraid. The one that's free is on the second floor, at the back. It looks onto the garden, so you won't hear the traffic.
That sounds ideal. And how much is the rent?
It was advertised at 105 pounds a week, but I've reduced it, because the room doesn't have its own bathroom. So it's 95 pounds a week.

Gas, electricity and water are all included, so there are no nasty surprises in winter. The only thing you'd pay for yourself is the internet. The tenants split that between them. It comes to about eight pounds each a month.
That seems fair. What about a deposit?
The last tenant paid 300 pounds, but I've put it up for new people, so it's 400 pounds now. You get all of it back at the end, as long as there's no damage.
Fine. And when could I move in?
Well, the room is empty from the 4th, but the painters are coming in, so it won't be ready until the 14th of September. Would that suit you?
That's perfect, actually. My current contract finishes on the 12th, so I'd have a couple of days to spare. Oh, one more thing. I cycle everywhere. Is there anywhere I could keep a bike?
Yes, there's a lockable shed at the side of the house. Everybody keeps their bicycles in there, and I'll give you your own key.
Brilliant. And what are the other people like?

There are three others at the moment. Two are postgraduates, and the third is a nurse who works nights, so you'll hardly ever see her. They're all very friendly. They take it in turns to cook on Sundays, but nobody is forced to join in.
Is the kitchen big enough for everyone? I do quite a lot of cooking, and I'd hate to be in the way.
It's the biggest room in the house, to be honest. We put in a new cooker last spring, and there's a large table where people eat together if they want to. Nobody has ever complained about space.
That sounds great. Could I come and have a look at the room?
Of course. I'm showing it to people on Saturday morning. Would 10.00 suit you?
Oh, I'm working at a cafe until half past ten on Saturdays. Could I come a bit later?
Let's say 11.30, then. I'll put your name down. And if you can bring a reference from your present landlord, that would be very helpful.
I'll do that. Thanks very much, Mrs Pryor. I'll see you on Saturday.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.context: A university librarian explains the library's services to new students.
script: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the Ashworth Library. My name's Dana Whitfield, and I'm one of the subject librarians here. I know you've been given a great deal of information this week, so I'll try to keep this short and useful. I'll tell you about opening hours and borrowing, and then we'll walk through the building together.

First, opening hours. During term, the library is open from 8 in the morning until 10 at night on weekdays, and from 10 until 6 at weekends. Now, some of you may have heard that we stay open all night. That's only true during the exam period, which starts in week 10. For those three weeks we open 24 hours a day. We did try opening until 2 a.m. all year round, but hardly anyone came, so we stopped.

Next, borrowing. As undergraduates, you can have up to 20 books out at any one time. Postgraduates can borrow 30. Last year the limit was only 10, but students told us that wasn't enough, so we changed it. Books are normally lent for four weeks, and you can renew them. You used to have to come to the help desk to do that, and some people still ring us up, but the easiest way is to use the library app. It takes about ten seconds, and it will even remind you before the due date.

If you do forget, ordinary books cost you 20 pence a day. The ones to watch are the short-loan books. These are the popular titles from reading lists, which you can only keep for 24 hours, and if you bring one back late you pay a fine for every hour, not every day. That adds up very fast. And if your unpaid fines reach 10 pounds, we'll block your account until you've paid.

We also run free workshops throughout the year. There are sessions on using the printers, on finding journal articles, and on avoiding plagiarism. If you can only manage one, I'd really recommend the one on avoiding plagiarism. Universities take it very seriously, and the rules are not always what people expect. The workshops are listed on the library website, and there is no need to book.
Right, let's make a move. I'll describe the building as we go. The lift is on my left, but we'll take the stairs, so follow me.

We'll start at the top. The third floor is our silent reading room. You may be told it used to be group study space, and that's right, but those rooms have moved, so please don't talk up there. If you need to make a call or eat a sandwich, go down a level or two.

On the second floor, you'll find the group study rooms. There are twelve of them, and you can book one for up to three hours using the app. They have whiteboards and screens, so they're ideal for project work.

The first floor houses the language learning centre. It has headphones, audio equipment and a good collection of films and books in more than thirty languages. Even if you aren't studying a language, it's worth a visit. It's also the quietest place to read a newspaper.

Down on the ground floor, as you'd expect, you'll find the main entrance and the issue desk, and beside that the computer suite. That's where the printers are too. Each of you gets 10 pounds of free printing credit, which you can top up at the machines. We also have an annex, in the old chapel next door, but I'm afraid that's closed for refurbishment until January, so please ignore the signs that point there.

Finally, the basement. This is where we keep the rare books and the university archive. You can't just walk in. You have to ask at the desk, and you need to leave your bag in a locker, but the staff are very helpful and some of the material down there is fascinating. There are letters, maps and photographs going back to the university's foundation.
Well, that's the whole library. Are there any questions before we go and have a proper look around?

parts.title: Part 3
parts.context: Two students and their tutor discuss the design of a psychology experiment on attention.
script: Come in, both of you, and sit down. Right, you wanted to talk about your attention project. How is it going?
Quite well, Dr Marsh. We've settled on a topic at last. We want to find out whether a phone buzzing nearby affects how well people concentrate.
Interesting. What made you choose that?
Well, I'd read an article about it over the summer, but to be honest that wasn't the reason.
It was really because of me. I noticed in the library that I couldn't read a page without checking my phone, even when nothing had happened. Freya thought it would make a good study.
Good. Personal experience is a fine starting point, as long as the design is rigorous. So tell me about the plan.
We'd like to recruit forty first-year psychology students and test them one at a time in the lab.

Forty is perfectly adequate for a student project, so don't worry about the number. My concern is that they'd all be psychology students. Many will already have taken part in experiments, some will guess what you're testing, and that could bias your results.
That's a fair point. Could we put up posters in other departments as well?
Yes, do that, and offer a small reward, perhaps a coffee voucher. Now, how will you signal the notification?
We thought of using a ringtone, and letting people choose their own.
I'd avoid that. Different phones, different volumes, and you lose control of the conditions. A standard vibration is much better, the same for everybody.
Okay, a vibration it is. Another worry is that some people are glued to their phones and others hardly use them. That must affect the results.
Could we ask everyone to switch their phones off for a week beforehand?

That's unrealistic, and you'd never get volunteers. It's much simpler to give each participant a short questionnaire at the end about their usual habits. Then you can take it into account when you analyse the data.
Right. And for the task, we'd been thinking of a word search. You know, finding hidden words in a grid.
I'd steer clear of those. Everyone finds them easy, so you'd get near-perfect scores in every condition and you wouldn't see any difference. It's called a ceiling effect.
I see. So what would work better?
Let's fix the groups first. How many conditions were you thinking of?
Two. One group with the phone buzzing, and one without.
Hmm. Then you can't tell whether it's the buzz that matters, or simply having a phone nearby. I'd add a third group, with the phone on the desk but silent. So three groups.
Proofreading works well. Give them a text with deliberate mistakes in it and ask them to find as many as they can. You can score it objectively.
Proofreading, that's perfect. Owen, we could hide spelling and punctuation errors in a page from a magazine.
How long should they have? 10 minutes?
I'd say 12 minutes. Ten is too short for a text of 500 words, and any longer and people get bored.
That's too many. They'd feel defeated. Hide 24. That's enough to avoid a ceiling effect, but it's still manageable.
Right. We'll need a quiet room for the testing, won't we? The lab is booked most afternoons.
Ask the technician about the small seminar room on the first floor. It has no windows, so people won't be distracted by anything outside.
Is there anything else we need to do before we start testing?
Yes, the ethics form. You can't test anybody until your plan has been approved by the department's ethics committee. It meets on the first Monday of every month, so get your form in early.
We'll do it this week. Thanks, Dr Marsh.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.context: A lecturer talks about the domestication of the horse and its effects on human societies.
script: Good afternoon, everyone. Today I want to talk about one of the most important partnerships in human history, the one between people and horses. Specifically, I'm going to look at when and how horses were domesticated, and what that did to human societies.

For a long time, the question of when this happened was surprisingly hard to answer, because the bones of a domesticated horse look almost exactly like those of a wild one. Early scholars guessed at around 6,000 years ago, but the evidence we have now suggests something closer to 5,000, on the grasslands of Central Asia and eastern Europe. So how do we know?

Three kinds of evidence have been particularly useful. The first is dental. When a horse is ridden with a bit, made of bone, leather or metal, the bit rubs against the front teeth and leaves distinctive wear. Examining skulls under a microscope, researchers can recognise these marks, and a horse's teeth are one of the best clues we have. The second kind comes from chemistry. Traces of mares' milk have been found inside ancient pottery, which tells us that people were keeping horses and milking them, and not only hunting them for meat. The third is genetic. When scientists compare the genomes of modern horses with those of ancient animals, they find that breeders selected for genes associated with strong backs, which made riding possible, and also for calm behaviour.

Now, what difference did all of this make? Let's start with speed and distance. A person on foot can manage around 30 kilometres in a day, and a cart pulled by oxen is no faster. A rider on a good horse could cover 100 kilometres. Think about what that means for communication, for trade and for how large a territory a single ruler could control.

Warfare changed too, although not at once. The first horses in battle pulled light chariots, which were expensive, needed flat ground and could be used only by wealthy elites. Around 3,000 years ago, riding took over, and mounted soldiers became far more mobile. But fighting from horseback was still difficult and dangerous, because there was nothing to support the rider's feet. The arrival of the stirrup, much later, gave the rider a stable seat, and that made cavalry a devastating force.

Let's turn to the wider effects on society. First, trade. With horses, goods and ideas moved much faster, and long-distance trade expanded across Asia and Europe. You might expect that the main beneficiaries were merchants, but the real change was in the way that people lived. Herders could now manage far larger herds, because a mounted shepherd can control animals over huge distances, so grassland communities grew richer and more powerful.

Large empires also depended on horses to hold themselves together. Several of them built networks of relay stations, where fresh horses and messengers waited, so that an order could cross a continent in days rather than months. Without this, governing such a vast area would simply have been impossible.

Farming was changed as well, although this came much later. For centuries, horses could not be used efficiently for ploughing, because the old harness pressed on their throats and they could not breathe properly when pulling a heavy load. In medieval Europe, the horse collar solved this problem, so that a horse could pull with its shoulders instead. Horses are faster than oxen, so more land could be ploughed, and that helped to raise food production.

Finally, let's bring the story up to date. In the twentieth century, engines replaced horses in transport, in farming and in war, and horse populations fell sharply in many countries. Today, most horses in wealthy countries are kept for leisure, for racing, riding and sport, although some are used in therapy programmes for people with disabilities.
In the second half of the lecture, I'll look at what the horse meant for particular cultures. But before that, any questions so far?

passages.title: The Story of Glass
paras: A  Glass is so familiar that it is easy to forget how strange a substance it is. It is made mostly from sand, yet it is transparent. It behaves like a solid, but its atoms lack the neat, repeating pattern found in a crystal, which is why scientists sometimes describe it as a frozen liquid. Long before anyone learned to manufacture it, people knew glass in a natural form. Obsidian, a black glass created when volcanic lava cools very quickly, was chipped into blades and arrowheads in the Stone Age. It was traded across hundreds of kilometres, because nothing else took such a sharp edge.

B  The earliest man-made glass appeared in Mesopotamia and Egypt some 3,500 years ago, and it was used not for windows or drinking vessels but for jewellery. Craftsmen produced small beads and inlays, coloured with copper and cobalt to imitate lapis lazuli and turquoise, stones that were far more costly than the glass itself. Vessels followed soon afterwards. To make one, a workshop wound threads of soft glass around a core of clay and dung shaped like the finished pot, rolled the surface smooth, and scraped out the core once the glass had cooled. The method was slow and the results were small, so glass remained a luxury owned by temples and royal courts. Many workshops guarded their recipes closely, passing them from parent to child.

C  Everything changed in the first century BC, probably somewhere in the eastern Mediterranean, when an unknown craftsman discovered that a gather of molten glass on the end of a hollow iron tube could be inflated like a bubble. Glassblowing was at least ten times faster than the old core method, and it needed far less fuel and labour. Within a few generations, ordinary households across the Roman Empire could afford glass bottles, bowls and lamp chimneys, and merchants began to ship wine and oil in glass containers rather than in pottery jars. Roman workshops also learned to cast panes for windows. These were thick and uneven, and they appeared mainly in bathhouses and the villas of the rich.

D  After the collapse of Roman authority in the west, glass-making did not disappear, but it changed. In northern Europe, where the soda used by Mediterranean workshops was hard to obtain, craftsmen turned to the ash of burned beech wood and bracken. The glass this produced was greenish and full of bubbles, yet it was cheap, and it supplied the coloured panels for the stained-glass windows of the great medieval cathedrals. Meanwhile, in the Islamic world, workshops in Syria and Persia developed enamelled and gilded glass that was admired as far away as China.

E  By the thirteenth century, the Italian city of Venice had become the centre of European glass-making. In 1291 the authorities ordered every furnace to move to the island of Murano. The official reason was the danger of fire in a city of wooden buildings, but the move also made it easier to watch over the industry's secrets. Glassworkers there were respected and well paid, but they were forbidden to leave the republic, and those who fled could expect to be pursued. In the fifteenth century, a Murano master perfected cristallo, a remarkably clear glass made by purifying the ash and adding manganese to remove the greenish tint. Venetian mirrors and goblets were prized by every court in Europe.

F  Secrecy could not last for ever. Venetian workers did emigrate, carrying their techniques to Bohemia, the Low Countries and England. In England, much of the timber had been consumed by furnaces, and in 1615 a royal proclamation forbade the use of wood as fuel, which pushed glass-makers to switch to coal. Coal-fired furnaces burned hotter, but the pots had to be covered to keep soot away from the glass, and the result was a denser, heavier material. Experiments in the 1670s added lead oxide to the mixture and produced a brilliant glass that rang when struck and sparkled when cut. Lead crystal became the fashionable tableware of the eighteenth century.

G  Industrialisation turned glass from a craft into a mass product. In the nineteenth century, machines for pressing glass into moulds made cheap tableware possible, and by the early twentieth century automatic machines could turn out thousands of identical bottles an hour, replacing a workforce that had relied on the lung power of skilled blowers. The last great advance came in the 1950s with the float process. Molten glass is poured onto a bath of liquid tin, where it spreads out and sets with perfectly flat surfaces, so costly grinding and polishing are no longer needed. Today almost all of the world's window glass is made this way. It is a fitting end to a story that began with a lucky accident and a closely guarded secret: a material that was once worth more than gemstones now fills the walls of every city.

passages.title: Trees for the Street
paras: A  For most of the twentieth century, the trees that lined city streets were treated as decoration, to be planted when budgets allowed and removed when they became inconvenient. That attitude is changing. A growing body of research suggests that urban trees do real work: they shade pavements and buildings, intercept rainfall, trap airborne dust and may even improve the health of the people who live beside them. But enthusiasm can be a poor guide to planning. The benefits vary enormously from one tree to another, and they depend on decisions about where to plant, what to plant and who will pay to look after it afterwards.

B  The most widely publicised benefit is cooling. A tree does not simply block the sun. Through its leaves, a large specimen releases hundreds of litres of water vapour on a hot day, and the evaporation draws heat from the surrounding air. In a study of paved squares in the city of Valmont, surfaces beneath mature trees were as much as 20 degrees cooler than unshaded ones at midday. Not all species perform equally, however. Species with dense crowns and large leaves cast the deepest shade and release the most moisture, whereas those with thin, open canopies do much less. The effect on buildings can be considerable. Researchers at the Tarnby Institute calculated that well-placed trees could reduce the cost of air-conditioning in nearby offices and homes by around 15 per cent in summer.

C  The picture is less straightforward for air quality. Leaves, particularly rough or hairy ones, capture fine particles from traffic and industry, and a belt of trees beside a busy road can lower the dust that reaches nearby windows. Yet some species give off volatile organic compounds, chemicals that react with exhaust fumes in sunlight to form ozone. A city that planted large numbers of such trees in an already polluted district could, in theory, make the air worse. Pollen creates another difficulty. Planners once favoured male trees because they drop no messy fruit, but they release far more pollen, and allergy specialists now advise against planting too many of them. On the other side of the ledger, a survey of 4,000 hospital patients in Valmont found that people who lived on greener streets recovered more quickly from surgery.

D  Choosing which tree to plant is therefore a delicate matter. For decades, many cities planted a single, reliable species along entire avenues. The result was often spectacular, until disease arrived. When a fungal infection swept through the elms of one northern city in the 1970s, tens of thousands of trees died within a few years and entire streets were left bare. To avoid a repeat, many planners now follow the so-called 10-20-30 rule, which says that no more than 10 per cent of the trees in a city should belong to one species, no more than 20 per cent to one genus and no more than 30 per cent to one family. Climate change adds a further complication. Trees planted today must survive the conditions of 2080, and some native species, adapted to cooler summers, may not. This has prompted a debate between those who insist on local species for the sake of wildlife and those willing to import hardier trees from warmer regions.

E  Even the best species will fail if it is planted in the wrong place. The ground beneath a city street is hostile: soil is compacted by traffic, packed with cables and pipes, and contaminated by winter road salt. The average life of a street tree in a large city is often put at under twenty years, whereas a tree in woodland may stand for centuries. Engineers have responded with new techniques. In some cities, trees are planted in soil cells, strong plastic frames buried beneath the pavement, which hold up the paving slabs while leaving room for roots to spread without being crushed. The system works, but it is not cheap, and it has to be designed into a street before the road is built.

F  Cost is the question that councils ask first. Planting a young tree is relatively inexpensive, but the bills that follow are not. New trees need regular watering for the first three years, formal pruning, and inspection for disease and structural weakness. Roots can lift paving slabs and block drains, and the owner of a falling branch may face a claim for damages. Against this, several economic studies have estimated that every pound spent on street trees returns between two and five pounds in benefits, such as lower energy costs, higher property values and reduced flooding. Critics counter that many of these benefits are hard to measure and that those who gain, such as property owners, are often not the ones who pay, which is the taxpayer in general.

G  There is also a question of fairness. Wealthy districts generally have more tree cover than poorer ones, even though poorer neighbourhoods are often the hottest and most polluted. Several councils have therefore concentrated new planting in such districts. The results have been mixed. Where residents were consulted, and given a say in which trees to plant, survival rates were high. Where trees were simply installed by contractors, vandalism and neglect were common, and some residents feared that greener streets would push up rents and drive them out. The lesson, according to one planner, is that a tree is not an object but a long-term relationship, and that the people who live beside it need to want it to thrive.

passages.title: Does Choice Really Overload Us?
paras: A  It is an article of faith in modern consumer society that more choice is better. A typical supermarket now stocks some 30,000 products, and a shopper can choose among dozens of mobile phone tariffs, hundreds of television channels and countless brands of shampoo. Freedom to choose is treated as the very essence of a free life. Yet since the turn of the century, a very different claim has gained ground: that too much choice makes people unhappy, unable to decide and less likely to buy anything at all. The claim rests largely on one celebrated experiment. Researchers at the University of Lindholm set up a tasting table in a delicatessen, first with six varieties of marmalade and then with twenty-four. The larger display drew more visitors, but only three per cent of those who stopped went on to buy a jar, compared with thirty per cent at the smaller display.

B  The result was irresistible to journalists and consultants, and it spread rapidly. Similar findings appeared to emerge from studies of retirement savings, which suggested that the more investment funds an employer offered, the fewer employees signed up for a pension scheme at all. Self-help writers began to preach the virtues of simplicity, and several large retailers reduced their ranges, with one chain claiming that its sales of shampoo rose after it dropped a third of its brands. I do not claim that these retailers were wrong; in their particular circumstances, they may well have been right. My objection is to the way a single experiment has hardened into received wisdom, and has been quoted in boardrooms and government departments as if it were a law of nature.

C  For anyone who takes the trouble to examine the evidence, the law turns out to be rather less firm. When other teams tried to repeat the marmalade study, many failed to find the same result. In some cases, bigger displays produced more sales. A review that combined the results of ninety-nine experiments, involving more than 50,000 participants, concluded that the average effect of having more options was close to zero. That figure conceals huge variation: in some studies, choice overload was dramatic, and in others, larger ranges clearly helped. A finding that sometimes appears and sometimes does not is not a law. It is a clue that something else is going on.

D  What that something is has become clearer in recent years. Overload seems most likely when the options are very similar and hard to compare, when the chooser has no clear idea of what he or she wants, and when time is short. Imagine selecting a pension from forty near-identical funds with an hour before the deadline. Contrast that with a buyer who knows she wants a green sofa with oak legs. Faced with a showroom of two hundred sofas, she is delighted rather than daunted, because her preferences let her ignore almost all of them. Experts behave in the same way: a keen cyclist can scan a wall of saddles in seconds. It is tempting to blame the internet for making these problems worse, but I know of no evidence that settles the matter either way.

E  Another popular idea divides people into maximisers, who need to find the very best option, and satisficers, who are content with one that is good enough. Questionnaire studies report that maximisers are less satisfied with their purchases and more prone to regret. Yet there is a problem of cause and effect. Perhaps maximising makes people unhappy; but perhaps unhappy, anxious people are more inclined to search for perfection. The labels themselves are also suspect, because the same person can be a maximiser when buying a camera and a satisficer when buying socks. I am not convinced that human beings can be reliably sorted into two types in this way, and I suspect that the scales used to do so measure little more than general anxiety.

F  None of this means that choice never causes problems. A badly designed menu of options can confuse and exhaust. The question is what to do about it. One response is to cut the number of options, or to set a sensible default, as many governments now do with pension schemes. Defaults have their place, but removing options is not a neutral act. Every item struck from the list is something that a minority of customers wanted, and a narrow range quietly excludes people whose tastes are unusual. A better approach, in my view, is to help people to cope with abundance rather than to take it away. Search filters, honest rankings and comparison tools allow a shopper to narrow a hundred options to five in a minute, and they leave the final decision where it belongs.

G  The real lesson of the choice overload literature, then, is not that less is more. It is that the way in which options are presented matters at least as much as how many there are. That is a more modest message than the one that made headlines, and it is also a more useful one. It may well be that the effect is stronger in some cultures than in others; the evidence so far comes overwhelmingly from North America and Europe. Until that gap is filled, anyone who tells you that fewer choices will make you happier is selling something.
